content:
Sustained throughput

Objective

The goal of this benchmark was to find the maximum number of sustained starting process instances per second of a “typical” process definition. This gives an indication of a “real world scenario” performance. We want to know the amount of process instances that can be handled concurrently and want to find out the latency numbers between messages passed and processed.

Note: Note: this model is similar in shape (multiple tasks, timers, gateway) to the ‘typical’ process used in Camunda performance posts

The typical process definition consists of 10 service tasks. Each worker takes a dummy 200ms to complete. Each service task executes a simple FEEL expression to dynamically determine the job worker id. Furthermore there are two timers of 1 minute each and a gateway is also included. This means the theoretical duration of a process instance is 2x 1 minute + 10x200ms = 122 seconds.

Each instance is started with the following variable payload of approximately 100 bytes:

Test setup

Two tests were performed using the same Kafka cluster of 3x2CPU with 8GB memory each. The first run was with 1 engine node and the second run was with 2 engine nodes.

  • Partitions: 12
  • Threads: 6 for each node
  • Worker and starter node: 4CPU, 2 threads for workers
  • Durability: acks=all, idempotence=true, broadcast updates = true
  • Other: Kafka batch=262,144, linger=50 ms, commit interval=100 ms, poll=50 ms
  • Latency is measured as the time passed between the producing of a Kafka message and the reception and processing on another node

For each run, we slowly increased the number of process instances started. After each increase we waited until the increased number of process instances started to finish. This explains the “staircase” for the process instance throughput. I kept increasing the number of jobs until the latency “exploded” indicating the engine or Kafka could no longer keep up.

Results with 1 engine node

Graph Analysis

  • Process instance throughput (bottom-left graph): Shows the staircase ramp-up of process start rates. Sustained throughput climbs to over 850 PI/s before instability appears.
  • Flow Object throughput (bottom-right graph): Peaks around 12,500 flow nodes per second, matching the expected factor (10 service tasks + 2 timers + gateway per process).
  • Latency percentiles (top graphs):
  • Stable phase: P50 latency stays around 200–300 ms, P95 and P99 under 500 ms.
  • Saturation point (~11:15): Latencies shoot up, with P99 exceeding 800 ms, showing the engine or Kafka reached max sustainable throughput.
  • Process duration (top-middle graph): Average process duration aligns closely with the theoretical 122 s baseline during stable load with a value of around 124 seconds. This aligns nicely with the given latencies, confirming timers and worker delays are respected. At overload, average duration rises slightly before leveling out.
  • Process instance totals (bottom-middle graph): Over 1 million instances were started and finished, with both “started” and “finished” lines tracking steadily — until the overload point, where completion lagged.
  • At peak there were over 100,000 active processes being maintained by the single engine node.

Results with 2 engine nodes

Note: Above graph is for 1 node, so the throughput numbers should be doubled:

  • Throughput: Plateaued around ~1,600–1,700 PI/s per cluster (each node contributing ~800–850 PI/s, graphs show per-node throughput). Almost doubling showing horizontal scalability
  • Latency:
    P50 remained ~200–250 ms
    P95 ~400–500 ms
    P99 ~600–800 ms
    Even at doubled throughput, latency profiles were almost identical to the 1-node run.
  • Process duration: Again stable around theoretical baseline, showing that scaling horizontally does not aﬀect business-level timing.
  • Scaling behavior: Throughput nearly doubled when moving from 1 → 2 nodes, proving linear scalability for this workload.
